metadata.lab_title: Models, Errors, Loss, Optimization, and Learning

answers.Q1: The global error measures how far off all the predictions are from the actual data points combined. It's the sum of all the squared errors, so bigger differences get penalized more heavily.
answers.Q2: Changing the slope would change the angle of the line, and changing the intercept would move it up or down. Both would affect how well the line fits the data, changing the total error.
answers.Q3: The residual lines show the vertical distance between each data point and the predicted line. They help visualize the error at each specific point rather than just seeing the total error.
answers.Q4: Yes, you can have a small global error even with some large individual errors if most of the points are very close to the line. The squared errors from the many close points can outweigh a few larger errors.
answers.Q5: An extreme outlier would pull the best-fit line toward it because of the squared error penalty. The global error would increase significantly because that one point would contribute a large squared error.
answers.Q6: We started by trying random values, then noticed the error feedback and started moving in the direction that decreased error. We adjusted m first to get the slope roughly right, then adjusted b to shift the line up or down.
answers.Q7: Our best guess was pretty close to the global minimum - within about 0.2 for both m and b. The MSE landscape showed us that the error surface is smooth with one clear minimum, which made it easier to find.
answers.Q8: This is similar to ML training because the algorithm only sees the loss value, not the actual data. It has to adjust parameters blindly based only on whether the error goes up or down, just like we did.
answers.Q9: We used a combination of systematic search and following the warm/cold feedback. We started with x=0, then tried negative and positive values to see which direction improved.
answers.Q10: The warmer/colder feedback was really helpful - it told us whether we were moving in the right direction. We used it to narrow down the search range and focus on promising areas.
answers.Q11: Yes, we could still find a minimum using just the table. We'd look for the pattern of which x values give lower f(x) and systematically search in that direction, similar to binary search.
answers.Q12: We started by sampling points in a grid pattern to get an overview. After finding a high point, we sampled nearby points to see if we could find an even higher peak in that region.
answers.Q13: We can see 4 local peaks in the landscape. Our group spent most time near the tallest peak in the upper right, but we did explore near two other peaks before settling on the highest one.
answers.Q14: We were pretty close to the global maximum - our best sample was at (2.1, 3.4) with height 4.2, and the true global peak was at (2.3, 3.6) with height 4.5, so we were off by about 0.3 in position.
answers.Q15: This is similar to ML optimization because loss landscapes can have many local minima. A model might get stuck in a local minimum if it only explores one region, missing the global minimum where performance would be much better.

questions.Q1: In your own words, what does 'global error' or 'loss' measure in this plot?
questions.Q2: If we changed the slope or intercept of the line, how would that change the loss?
questions.Q3: How do the residual lines (the dashed vertical lines) help you understand the local error at each point?
questions.Q4: Can you make the global error small even if a few points still have relatively large errors? Describe a situation where this happens and why.
questions.Q5: Suppose you add one very extreme outlier point far away from the others. Predict how this will affect the best-fit line and the global error.
questions.Q6: Describe how your guesses for (m, b) moved over time. Did you follow any systematic strategy?
questions.Q7: Look at the MSE landscape plot. How close was your best guess to (a) the approximate global minimum on the grid, and (b) the least-squares solution from the data? What does this tell you about optimizing only based on the global error?
questions.Q8: In our earlier line-fitting exercise, you could see the data, the line, and the residuals. In this game, you only saw the MSE. How is this situation similar to how many machine learning models are trained?
questions.Q9: What strategies did your group use to choose new values of x within the allowed range?
questions.Q10: How did the 'warmer/colder' feedback influence your choices?
questions.Q11: Imagine that even the scatter plot of your guesses was hidden, and you only saw the table of (x, f(x)). Would you still be able to find a good minimum? How?
questions.Q12: Describe your group's strategy for choosing new (x, y) locations. How did you decide where to sample next after finding a high point?
questions.Q13: Look at the revealed landscape. How many local peaks can you see? Did your group spend most of its time near one peak, or did you explore multiple regions?
questions.Q14: Compare your best sample to the true global peak shown on the plot. Were you close to the global maximum, or did you end up stuck near a local maximum?
questions.Q15: Explain how this mountain-peak search is similar to what happens in machine learning when an algorithm is trying to optimize a loss function that has many 'bumps' (local minima or maxima). What risks does a model face if it only explores one region of the loss landscape?
